For Ellis, a pitcher whose season line had been steady but not spectacular, the timing couldn’t have been sharper. The A’s now ride a two-game win streak into the ALCS, their record sitting at three wins and one loss in the postseason. Eric Taveras, whose fourth-inning home run provided one of the few offensive highlights in a game dominated by pitching, summed up the mood in the dugout. "Man, what John did out there... that was next level," he said. "When your ace goes out and dominates like that in a playoff game, it changes everything. Now we've got momentum, and the whole team's feeding off that energy. You could feel it in the dugout—like, if he's bringing that kind of fire, how can the rest of us not step up?"

Taveras’ home run, his second of the series, was a solo shot in the fourth inning, part of a night where he went one-for-four with one RBI. It wasn’t a barrage of offense, but it didn’t need to be. Ellis’ performance rendered every run a luxury, not a necessity. Back in Oakland, the buzz was palpable. Rick Walker, tuning in from Fruitvale, caught the game on the radio. "I heard about John Ellis' shutout on the radio this morning—what a performance!" he said. "It’s got me thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to make a serious playoff run this year." Rafael Pilgrim echoed the sentiment: "I heard about John Ellis' shutout—nine innings, no runs. It’s got people here in Fruitvale buzzing, thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to go deep in the playoffs."

============================================================ By Anthony Raines | Bay Tribune Sports The first thing that jumps out on Danny Horn's postseason card is the zero in the home run column. Through forty-two at-bats this October, Oakland's center fielder is hitting a meager .190, with just three runs batted in and a slugging percentage that would make a light-hitting middle infielder blush. For a player expected to anchor the A's lineup, those numbers are hard to ignore. "Look, I know my numbers haven’t been where I want them this postseason," Horn admitted in a quiet moment before Game 1 of the World Series. "But I’m grinding every day. This team’s got heart, and I’m gonna do everything I can to help us bring home that championship."

The sentiment is admirable, but the Phillies’ pitching staff won’t care about heart when Horn steps to the plate. His struggles are amplified by the success of his teammates. Eric Taveras is hitting .359 with four home runs. Vladimir Gonzalez has matched Taveras' power output while batting .286. Ernesto Quintero, often hitting behind Horn, has three homers and a .324 average. In a lineup that has otherwise thrived, Horn’s slump stands out like a sore thumb. "Danny Horn’s been grinding, and I respect that," manager Deacon Seymour said. "The numbers don’t tell the whole story—he’s a guy who shows up every day, puts in the work, and keeps his head in the game. Right now, he’s not finding the gaps, but I’ve seen him turn it around before."

Trenton Nawan, a resident of Jack London, watched the game with a mix of concern and investment. "I've seen the Oaks struggle in their preseason performance, it's got me a bit worried about how they'll do this season. As someone who lives in Jack London, I'm really invested in seeing them succeed," he said, his brow furrowed in concern. The Oaks' preseason opener ended in a loss, with a record of 0-1 and a streak of L1. Austin Reaves led the team with 22 points, 6 assists, and 6 rebounds, while AJ Dybantsa added 18 points and 11 rebounds. Despite the loss, the team remains optimistic, with Coach Wilson Shepard emphasizing the importance of preseason as a time to figure things out.

The A’s have managed to win despite Horn’s struggles, but the margin for error becomes razor-thin in the World Series. Game 1 starter Arturo Ramos, who carries a 1.93 ERA into tonight’s contest, knows the stakes. "Numbers don’t always tell the whole story—he’s got the kind of at-bats that wear pitchers down," Ramos said of Horn. "We’re not worried. When it clicks for him, it’s gonna be big." The question isn’t just whether Horn can turn it around—it’s whether the A’s can survive another series if he doesn’t. With Philadelphia’s rotation looking formidable on paper, Oakland may not have the luxury of carrying a slumping star. For a team chasing its seventh ring, the margin for error has never been smaller.
